1. Introduction

In this exposé we give the fundamental theorem which says, in a somewhat more precise form, that for a proper morphism \(f : X \to Y\) of schemes, and for a torsion abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the stalk of \(R^q f_* F\) at a geometric point of \(Y\) is isomorphic to the cohomology \(H^q(X_{\bar y}, F|X_{\bar y})\) of the fibre \(X_{\bar y}\).

We recall that for a proper morphism of paracompact spaces the analogous result is well known (GODEMENT II 4.11) and easy. It is much more delicate in the case of schemes. For example, the hypothesis that \(F\) be torsion is indeed necessary, contrary to what happens for paracompact spaces.

The proof proceeds in several steps: by more or less formal dévissage methods one reduces to the case where \(Y\) is noetherian, where the relative dimension of \(f\) is \(\leq 1\), and where the sheaf \(F\) is constant. To treat this special case, one uses the specialization theorem for the fundamental group (5.9), which is a non-abelian variant of the theorem stated above, and which can be proved directly in the special case under consideration (XIII 2).
2. An example

Let us show that the hypothesis that \(F\) be torsion is necessary: Let \(X\) be a non-singular surface over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(Y\) a non-singular curve over \(k\), and \(f : X \to Y\) a proper morphism whose generic fibre is smooth and whose geometric fibre at the geometric point \(\bar y\) of \(Y\) has an ordinary double point, and is irreducible. Let \(F\) be the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}_X\).

We recall the following fact: for an arbitrary point \(z\) of a scheme \(Z\), let \(i : z \to Z\) be the inclusion. We have \(H^1(Z, i_* \mathbb{Z}_z) = 0\) (IX 3.6 (i)). Now since \(X\) is normal, hence unibranch, it follows that \(\mathbb{Z}_X \simeq i_* \mathbb{Z}_x\), where \(i : x \to X\) is the inclusion of the generic point. Hence \(H^1(X, \mathbb{Z}_X) = 0\) and likewise \(R^1 f_* \mathbb{Z}_X = 0\). But I claim that for the geometric fibre \(X_o\) of \(X/Y\) with the ordinary double point we have \(H^1(X_o, \mathbb{Z}_{X_o}) \simeq \mathbb{Z}\) (*), which gives the counterexample, since \(\mathbb{Z}_{X_o} \simeq \mathbb{Z}_X|X_o\).

Let \(i_o : x_o \to X_o\) be the inclusion of the generic point of \(X_o\), and let \(Q\) be the singular point of \(X_o\). The curve \(X_o\) has two "branches" at \(Q\), and it follows that the stalk of \(i_{o*}(\mathbb{Z}_{x_o})\) at the point \(Q\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\). Outside \(Q\) the curve \(X_o\) is normal, and hence \(i_{o*}(\mathbb{Z}_{x_o}) \simeq \mathbb{Z}_{X_o}\) on \(X_o - Q\). We thus have an exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{X_o} \longrightarrow i_{o*}(\mathbb{Z}_{x_o}) \longrightarrow (\mathbb{Z})_Q \longrightarrow 0 , \] where the last term is the extension by \(0\) of the sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}\) at the point \(Q\). All three terms have an \(H^0\) isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}\), and \(H^1(X_o, i_{o*}(\mathbb{Z}_{x_o})) = 0\), whence \(H^1(X_o, \mathbb{Z}_{X_o}) = \mathbb{Z}\) by the exact cohomology sequence.

footnotes.html: (*) Compare, from the point of view of \(\pi_1\), with SGA 3 X (6, Exemples) and (1.6).

blocks.html: 3. Reminders on the non-abelian \(H^1\)

We shall briefly indicate some results on non-abelian cohomology that we will need in the sequel. We will omit most of the proofs, which are well known in various special cases, and which can be found in GIRAUD's thesis [1].

Let \(X\) be a scheme, and \(F\) a sheaf of groups on \(X\). For each \(X'/X\) étale, one defines a pointed set \(H^1(X', F)\), covariantly functorial in \(F\) and contravariantly in \(X'\). The \(H^1\) commutes with finite products of sheaves. If \(f : X \to Y\) is a morphism, one defines a sheaf of pointed sets (that is, with a distinguished section) \(R^1 f_* F\). It is the sheaf associated to the presheaf (of pointed sets) \(\mathcal{R}^1 F\), which, to each \(Y'/Y\) étale, associates the set \(H^1(X \times_Y Y', F)\).
We have the usual exact cohomology sequences, of which we shall content ourselves with indicating one:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1

Let \(0 \to F \xrightarrow{\ u\ } G\) be an injection of sheaves of groups, and let \(C = G/F\) be the sheaf of homogeneous sets under \(G\). We have an exact sequence of sheaves of pointed sets \[ 0 \longrightarrow f_* F \longrightarrow f_* G \longrightarrow f_* C \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } R^1 f_* F \xrightarrow{\ u^1\ } R^1 f_* G . \]

Of course, this exact sequence is obtained by passing to the sequence of sheaves associated to the exact sequence of presheaves whose value for \(Y'/Y\) étale is \[ 0 \longrightarrow F(X') \longrightarrow G(X') \longrightarrow C(X') \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } H^1(X', F) \longrightarrow H^1(X', G) , \] where \(X' = X \times_Y Y'\). The equivalence relation induced by \(\partial\) is the one given by the action of \(f_* G\) on \(f_* C\). As usual, one can make explicit the equivalence relation induced by \(u^1\) by means of the notion of "twisting" [1].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

Let \(X \xrightarrow{\ f\ } Y \xrightarrow{\ g\ } Z\) be morphisms of schemes. We have an exact sequence for each \(Z'/Z\) étale, setting \(Y' = Y \times_Z Z'\), \(X' = X \times_Z Z'\): \[ 0 \longrightarrow H^1(Y', f_* F) \longrightarrow H^1(X', F) \longrightarrow H^0(Y', R^1 f_* F) , \] whence, passing to the associated sheaves, an exact sequence of pointed sheaves on \(Z\): \[ 0 \longrightarrow (R^1 g_*) f_* F \longrightarrow R^1 (gf)_* F \longrightarrow g_* (R^1 f_*) F . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3

The family of functors of the form \(H^1(X', F)\), for \(X'\) étale over \(X\), and of the form \(R^1 f_* F\), for an arbitrary morphism \(f : X \to Y\), is effaceable; that is, there exists an injection \(F \xrightarrow{\ u\ } G\) such that the induced morphisms \(H^1(X', F) \to H^1(X', G)\) and \(R^1 f_* F \to R^1 f_* G\) are all zero. More precisely, there exists an injection \(F \xrightarrow{\ u\ } G\) such that each of the sets \(H^1(X', G)\), with \(X'\) étale over \(X\), and each of the pointed sheaves \(R^1 f_* G\), is zero. If \(X\) is noetherian and \(F\) is a constructible sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, then there exists such an injection, where moreover \(G\) is a sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups.

Proof. The first assertion is no doubt true in an arbitrary topos, but for the étale topology it is convenient to carry out the effacement with the "Godement resolution" \[ (3.4) \qquad F \longrightarrow G = \prod_{x \in X} i_{x*} i_x^* F , \] where \(x\) runs over the set of points of \(X\) and where \(i_x : \bar x \to X\) is a geometric point of \(X\) over \(x\). Note that for \(X'/X\) étale, we have \[ G(X') = \prod_{x \in X} (i_x^* F)(X' \times_X \bar x) = \prod_{x \in X} \Big( \prod_{\bar x'/\bar x} F_{\bar x'} \Big) , \] where the \(\bar x'\) are geometric points of \(X'\). Now it is clear that for each point of \(X'\) there is at least one \(\bar x'\) lying over it, whence \(F(X') \subset G(X')\) (VIII 3), so \(F \subset G\). On the other hand, an arbitrary étale \(\bar u / \bar x\) is a sum of spectra of separably closed fields, whence \(H^1(\bar u, \bar G) = 0\) for any sheaf \(\bar G\) on \(\bar x\). It then follows from 3.2 that \(H^1(X', i_{x*} i_x^* F) = 0\) for each \(X'/X\) étale, whence (since \(H^1\) commutes with products) \(H^1(X', G) = 0\), and likewise \(R^1 f_* G = 0\) for every \(f : X \to Y\), thanks to the description of \(R^1 f_*(G)\) as the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(Y' \mapsto H^1(X \times_Y Y', G)\).

Now suppose moreover that \(F\) is constructible and \(X\) noetherian. Then one sees immediately that there exists a finite set of points \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) of \(X\) such that the morphism \[ F \longrightarrow \prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} i_{x_i*} i_{x_i}^* F \] is already injective. The sheaf \(i_{x*} i_x^* F\) is a sheaf of ind-finite groups (IX 1.5), hence so is the finite product (IX 1.4 and 1.6 (iii)). Replacing \(G\) by this sheaf, one obtains the last assertion.
3.5. As in the case of abelian cohomology (treated in V 2.4), one can compute the \(H^1\) by the ČECH procedure [1].
4. The base change morphism

Let \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g'} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]_{g} } \] be a cartesian square of morphisms of schemes. From it one deduces a morphism of functors \(\varphi = \varphi_g\) \[ (4.1) \qquad g^* f_* \xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ } f'_* g'^* \] in the following way: to give such a morphism is equivalent to giving a morphism of functors \[ (4.1\ \mathrm{adj}) \qquad f_* \longrightarrow g_* f'_* g'^* , \] because \(g_*\) and \(g^*\) are adjoint. For this morphism we take the morphism \[ f_* \xrightarrow{\ (\mathrm{id} \to g'_* g'^*)\ } f_* g'_* g'^* = g_* f'_* g'^* , \] taking into account that \[ g_* f'_* = (gf')_* = (fg')_* = f_* g'_* . \] Note that there is another candidate for (4.1). Indeed, to give such a morphism is equivalent to giving \[ f'^* g^* f_* \longrightarrow g'^* \] and one can take \[ f'^* g^* f_* \simeq g'^* f^* f_* \xrightarrow{\ (f^* f_* \to \mathrm{id})\ } g'^* . \]
I do not know whether these two choices always coincide (*), and in any case we shall use only the first. We call it the base change morphism.

By restricting (4.1) to abelian sheaves (resp. sheaves of groups) one deduces a morphism \(\varphi^q = \varphi^q_g\) for each \(q \geq 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0, 1\)): \[ (4.2) \qquad g^*(R^q f_*) \xrightarrow{\ \varphi^q\ } (R^q f'_*) g'^* . \] Indeed, this amounts to the same thing as giving \[ (4.2\ \mathrm{adj}) \qquad (R^q f_*) \longrightarrow g_*(R^q f'_*) g'^* , \] and one has "obvious" morphisms \[ (R^q f_*) \xrightarrow{\ a\ } (R^q f_*) g'_* g'^* \xrightarrow{\ b\ } R^q (f g')_* g'^* = = R^q (gf')_* g'^* \xrightarrow{\ c\ } g^*(R^q f'_*) g'^* . \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.3

Suppose that \(g\) (hence \(g'\)) is a closed immersion. Then the morphisms \(b\) and \(c\) above are isomorphisms (VIII 5.7). It follows that (4.2) is essentially none other than the morphism \(a\) above, which is defined by applying \(R^q f_*\) to the canonical morphism \(F \to g'_* g'^* F\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.4

(Composition of base change morphisms).

(i) Let \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g'} \ar[d]^{f'} & X'' \ar[l]_{h'} \ar[d]^{f''} \\ S & S' \ar[l]_{g} & S'' \ar[l]_{h} } \] be a cartesian diagram of morphisms of schemes. Then the following diagram is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ (gh)^* f_* \ar[rr]^{gh} \ar[d]_{\wr} & & f''_* (g'h')^* \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ h^* g^* f_* \ar[r]^{h^*_* g} & h^* f'_* g'^* \ar[r]^{h^*_* g'^*} & f''_* h'^* g'^* } \] and the diagram with \(f_*, f'_*, f''_*\) replaced by \(R^q f_*, R^q f'_*, R^q f''_*\) is also commutative, in the natural domains of definition of the functors in question (cf. n° 3).

(ii) Let \[ \xymatrix{ Y \ar[d]_{e} & Y' \ar[l]_{g''} \ar[d]^{e'} \\ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g'} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]_{g} } \] be a cartesian diagram of morphisms of schemes. Then the following diagram is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ g^*(fe)_* \ar[rr] \ar@{=}[d] & & (f'e')_* g''^* \ar@{=}[d] \\ g^* f_* e_* \ar[r] & f'_* g'^* e_* \ar[r] & f'_* e'_* g''^* , } \] where the three horizontal arrows come from the base change homomorphisms for \(fe\), \(f\) and \(e\) respectively.
In the abelian case, the base change morphisms for \(fe\) are induced by a morphism of spectral sequences
\[ \xymatrix{ E_2^{p,q} = g^*(R^p f_*)(R^q e_*) F \ar@{=>}[r] \ar[d]_{\varphi} & g^* R^{p+q}(fe)_* F \ar[d]^{\varphi} \\ (R^p f'_*)(R^q e'_*) g''^* F \ar@{=>}[r] & R^{p+q}(f'e')_* g'^* F } \]

which, for the initial terms, is induced by the base change morphisms for \(e\) and \(f\); and for a sheaf of groups, one has a morphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & g^*(R^1 f_*) e_* F \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\varphi} & g^* R^1(fe)_* F \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\varphi} & g^* f_*(R^1 e_*) F \ar[d]_{\varphi} \\ 0 \ar[r] & (R^1 f'_*) e'_* g''^* F \ar[r] & R^1(f'e')_* g''^* F \ar[r] & f'_*(R^1 e'_*) g''^* F } \] We leave the proof to the reader.

footnotes.html: (*) Mr. DELIGNE has resolved this perplexity in the affirmative, in a substantially more general context, cf. Exp. XVII.

pages.title: 5. Statement of the main theorem and of some variants

blocks.html: 5. Statement of the main theorem and of some variants
The theorem is the following:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1

(Base change theorem for a proper morphism). Let \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g'} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]_{g} } \] be a cartesian diagram of schemes, with \(f\) proper.

  1. (i) Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets on \(X\). Then the morphism (4.1) \[ \varphi : g^* f_* F \longrightarrow f'_* g'^* F \] is bijective.
  2. (ii) Let \(F\) be a sheaf of groups (resp. of ind-finite groups) on \(X\). Then the morphism (4.2) \[ \varphi^1 : g^*(R^1 f_*) F \longrightarrow (R^1 f'_*) g'^* F \] is injective (resp. bijective).
  3. (iii) Let \(F\) be a torsion abelian sheaf on \(X\). Then the morphism (4.2) \[ \varphi^q : g^*(R^q f_*) F \longrightarrow (R^q f'_*) g'^* F \] is bijective for each \(q \geq 0\).

We shall first state some immediate consequences of the theorem. If \(S' = \xi\) is a geometric point of \(S\), so that a sheaf on \(\xi\) is determined by its global sections, we have \(H^0(\xi, R^q f'_* G) = H^q(X', G)\) for each sheaf \(G\) on \(X\), whence the following corollary (which is moreover essentially equivalent to (5.1)):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2

Let \(f : X \to S\) be proper, \(\xi \to S\) a geometric point, and \(X_\xi\) the fibre of \(f\) at the point \(\xi\).

  1. (i) If \(F\) is a sheaf of sets on \(X\), the canonical base change morphism \[ (f_* F)_\xi \longrightarrow H^0(X_\xi, F|X_\xi) \] is bijective.
  2. (ii) If \(F\) is a sheaf of groups (resp. of ind-finite groups), the base change morphism \[ R^1 f_*(F)_\xi \longrightarrow H^1(X_\xi, F|X_\xi) \] is injective (resp. bijective).
  3. (iii) If \(F\) is a torsion abelian sheaf, then for each \(q \geq 0\) the base change morphism \[ (R^q f_* F)_\xi \longrightarrow H^q(X_\xi, F|X_\xi) \] is bijective.
Taking into account (X 4.3) and (X 5.2), we find:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3

Under the conditions of (5.2), let \(n\) be the dimension of the fibre \(X_\xi\). Then for each torsion abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the stalk \((R^q f_* F)_\xi\) is zero for \(q > 2n\). If \(F\) is a \(p\)-torsion sheaf (\(p\) the characteristic of \(\xi\)), then the stalk of \(R^q f_*(F)\) at \(\xi\) is zero for \(q > n\).
We recall that one says that the relative dimension of \(X/S\) is \(\leq n\) if the dimension of each fibre is \(\leq n\). We thus have

blocks.label: 5.3 bis
blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3 bis

Let \(f : X \to S\) be proper and \(X/S\) of relative dimension \(\leq n\). Then \(R^q f_* F = 0\) if \(q > 2n\) for each torsion abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\). If \(S\) is of characteristic \(p\), and if \(F\) is a \(p\)-torsion abelian sheaf, then \(R^q f_* F = 0\) if \(q > n\).
By applying (5.1) to a morphism of spectra of separably closed fields, one obtains

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4

(Invariance of cohomology under base field change in the proper case). Let \(k \subset K\) be separably closed fields and \(X\) a scheme proper over \(\operatorname{Spec} k\). Let \(X' = X_K\). Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(X\) and \(F'\) the inverse image sheaf on \(X'\). Then

  1. (i) \[H^0(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^0(X', F') .\]
  2. (ii) If \(F\) is a sheaf of groups (resp. of ind-finite groups) \[ H^1(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^1(X', F') \] is injective (resp. bijective).
  3. (iii) If \(F\) is a torsion abelian sheaf, \[ H^q(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X', F') \] for every \(q\).
A slightly different variant of (5.2) is the following:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a henselian ring and let \(S' = s_o\) be the closed point. Let \(f : X \to S\) be proper. Set \(X_o = X'\), \(F_o = g'^* F\). Then we have:

  1. (i) \[H^0(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^0(X_o, F_o)\] for every sheaf of sets \(F\).
  2. (ii) \[H^1(X, F) \longrightarrow H^1(X_o, F_o)\] is injective (resp. bijective) for every sheaf of groups (resp. of ind-finite groups) \(F\).
  3. (iii) \[H^q(X, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X_o, F_o)\] for every torsion abelian sheaf \(F\), and every \(q\).

Indeed, this statement is only a special case of (5.2) if \(S\) is strictly local. Suppose (5.2) is known. Let \(\bar S\) be the strict localization of \(S\), \(\bar s\) the closed point of \(\bar S\), \(G\) the Galois group of \(\bar S/S\) (which is also the Galois group of \(\bar s/s_o\)). Then \(G\) acts on the stalks of the \(R^q\), and we have (with obvious notation) \[ H^0(X, F) \simeq H^0(\bar X, \bar F)^G \] \[ H^0(X_o, F_o) \simeq H^0(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)^G \] for a sheaf of sets \(F\), whence (i) since \(H^0(\bar X, \bar F) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^0(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)\) and the isomorphism obviously commutes with the action of \(G\).

If \(F\) is a sheaf of groups, one easily defines a morphism of exact sequences of pointed sets \[ (5.5.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & H^1(G, H^0(\bar X, \bar F)) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(X, F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(\bar X, \bar F)^G \ar[d] \\ 0 \ar[r] & H^1(G, H^0(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)) \ar[r] & H^1(X_o, F_o) \ar[r] & H^1(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)^G } \] where the outer vertical arrows are isomorphisms by (5.2). Let \(\alpha\), \(\beta \in H^1(X, F)\) be classes having the same image in \(H^1(X_o, F_o)\), and let \(F^\alpha\) be the sheaf obtained by twisting \(F\) by means of \(\alpha\) [1]. Let \(\beta'\) be the class in \(H^1(X, F^\alpha)\) corresponding to \(\beta\). Then, since the class \(\alpha'\) corresponding to \(\alpha\) is zero, the image of \(\beta'\) in \(H^1(X_o, (F^\alpha)_o)\) is zero.

Let us examine the diagram deduced from (5.5.1) by replacing \(F\) by \(F^\alpha\): one finds that the image of \(\beta'\) in \(H^1(\bar X, \bar F^\alpha)^G\) is zero, so that \(\beta'\) is the image of an element of \(H^1(G, H^0(\bar X, \bar F))\), and that this element must be zero. Hence \(\beta'\) is zero, i.e. \(\beta' = \alpha'\), whence \(\beta = \alpha\). This gives the injectivity of the morphism of (ii).

Now suppose that \(F\) is a sheaf of ind-finite groups, and let us prove the surjectivity of the arrow (ii). Now it suffices to prove that the functor \(F \mapsto H^1(X_o, F_o)\) is effaceable. Indeed, let \(0 \to F \xrightarrow{u} G\) be an injection that effaces this functor. Let \(C = G/F\). We have a morphism of exact sequences (4.4) \[ \xymatrix{ H^0(X, C) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(X, F) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{\varepsilon} & H^1(X, G) \ar[d] \\ H^0(X_o, C_o) \ar[r] & H^1(X_o, F_o) \ar[r]^{u^1_o} & H^1(X_o, G_o) } \] where the morphism \(u^1_o\) is zero, which indeed implies the surjectivity of \(\varepsilon\).

Let us prove that the functor \(F \mapsto H^1(X_o, F_o)\) is effaceable for sheaves \(F\) of ind-finite groups. Let \(F \xrightarrow{u} C\) be the "Godement resolution" (3.4). We have \[ H^1(G, H^0(\bar X_o, \bar C_o)) \simeq H^1(G, H^0(\bar X, \bar C)) \subset H^1(X, C) = 0 \] Moreover, we have the commutative square: \[ \xymatrix{ H^1(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r]^{\sim} \ar[d] & H^1(\bar X_o, \bar F_o) \ar[d] \\ 0 = H^1(\bar X, \bar C) \ar[r] & H^1(\bar X_o, \bar C_o) } \] (since \(H^1(\bar X, \bar C) = \varinjlim H^1(X', C) = 0\), \(X'/X\) étale), hence it is zero. We thus have a morphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & H^1(G, H^0(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(X_o, F_o) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{\beta} & H^1(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)^G \ar[d]^{\alpha^G} \\ 0 \ar[r] & & H^1(X_o, C_o) \ar[r] & H^1(\bar X_o, \bar C_o)^G } \] where \(\alpha^G\) is zero, which implies that \(\beta\) is also zero, whence effaceability.

Finally, let us prove assertion (iii) of (5.5): We have a morphism of spectral sequences \[ \xymatrix{ E_2^{p,q} = H^p(G, H^q(\bar X, \bar F)) \ar@{=>}[r] \ar[d] & H^n(X, F) \ar[d]^{\varphi} \\ H^p(G, H^q(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)) \ar@{=>}[r] & H^n(X_o, F_o) } \] By (5.2), the morphisms \(H^q(\bar X, \bar F) \longrightarrow H^q(\bar X_o, \bar F_o)\) are isomorphisms. This implies that \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism for \(E_2^{p,q}\), hence for the abutments, whence the result, q.e.d.

5.6. Let us examine (5.5) (i) and (ii) in the case where \(F\) is constant: Let \(F = T_X\) be a constant sheaf of sets on the scheme \(X\), with value \(T\). Then \(F(X)\) is none other than the set of locally constant maps from \(X\) to \(T\). If \(X_o\) is a subscheme of \(X\), and if \(T\) has at least two elements, one concludes that \(F(X) \to F(X_o)\) is bijective if and only if the map \(U \mapsto U_o = U \cap X_o\) from the set \(\theta(X)\) of subsets of \(X\) that are both open and closed to the analogous set \(\theta(X_o)\) is bijective. If the set \(\pi_o(X)\) of connected components of \(X\) is finite, this amounts to the same thing as saying that the map \(\pi_o(X_o) \longrightarrow \pi_o(X)\) is bijective. Thus, (5.5) (i) can also be reformulated in the following way (taking into account that in this case \(X_o\) is of finite type over a field, hence noetherian, hence \(\pi_o(X_o)\) is finite):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a henselian ring, \(s_o\) its closed point. Let \(f : X \to S\) be a proper morphism and \(X_o\) the closed fibre of \(X/S\). Then the map \(\pi_o(X_o) \to \pi_o(X)\) induced by \(X_o \to X\) is bijective.
(In particular, this implies that the set \(\pi_o(X)\) is finite). We shall prove (5.7) directly in the noetherian case:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.8

The statement (5.7) is true if \(S\) is noetherian (*).

Proof. In the noetherian case, \(\pi_o(X)\) is certainly finite, and by replacing \(X\) by a connected component one may assume that \(\pi_o(X)\) is a one-element set, that is, that \(X\) is connected and non-empty. One must show that then \(X_o\) is likewise connected and non-empty. Now the image of \(X\) in \(S\) is closed since \(f\) is proper, and non-empty since \(X\) is non-empty, hence contains \(s_o\), which explains why \(X_o\) is non-empty. Let \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} \ar[r]^{f'} & S' \ar[dl]^{\pi} \\ S & } \] be the Stein factorization of \(f\) (EGA III 4.3.3), so that \(S'/S\) is finite and \(S'\) is connected. One knows that each fibre of \(f'\) is connected and non-empty, and the space underlying \(X_o\) is the union of the spaces underlying the closed fibres of \(S'\). Everything thus comes down to showing that \(S'\) is the spectrum of a local ring. But since \(S\) is henselian, the ring \(A'\) of \(S'\) is a product of local rings (VII 4.1 (i)), hence \(A'\) is local since \(S'\) is connected, which proves 5.8.

5.9.0. Now suppose that \(F = G_X\) is a constant sheaf of groups, with value \(G\), where \(G\) is a finite group. Then \(H^1(X, G_X)\) classifies the principal Galois coverings of \(X\), with group \(G\) (VII 2.1). Corollary 5.5 (ii) says that the morphism \(X_o \to X\) induces a bijection between the sets of classes of these coverings. It thus follows, from the definition of the \(\pi_1\), that 5.5 (ii) for constant sheaves of finite groups (in the presence of (i)) is equivalent to:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.9

(Specialization theorem for the fundamental group). With the notation of (5.5), suppose \(X\) connected and non-empty. Then \(X_o\) is connected and non-empty, and if \(\bar x_o\) is a geometric point of \(X_o\), the morphism of fundamental groups \[ \pi_1(X_o, \bar x_o) \longrightarrow \pi_1(X, \bar x_o) \] is bijective.
On the other hand, by Galois theory (SGA V) the statement 5.9 (in the case where \(X_o\) is connected, which one may assume, thanks to 5.7) is equivalent to

blocks.label: 5.9 bis
blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.9 bis

Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a henselian ring, \(s_o\) the closed point of \(S\), \(f : X \to S\) a proper morphism, and \(X_o\) the closed fibre of \(X/S\). For a scheme \(Z\), let \(\operatorname{Et}(Z)\) denote the category of étale coverings of \(Z\). Then the restriction functor \[ \operatorname{Et}(X) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Et}(X_o) \] is an equivalence of categories.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.10

We recall that 5.9 has already been proved (SGA 1 X 2.1) in the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a complete noetherian local ring. Unfortunately one does not manage to use this result to prove 5.9 in general (*), and the proof of 5.9 given, in the present exposé and the following one, is very different from the one given in SGA 1 X.

5.11. One can give another "non-commutative" variant of (5.5) (ii), by using the theory of 2-cohomology of J. GIRAUD (cf. Thèse de J. GIRAUD, en préparation). Suppose \(S\) noetherian. Take a band \(L\) on \(X\), and suppose that \(L\) is locally realized (for the étale topology) by a sheaf of ind-finite groups. Consider the map \[ \varphi^{(2)} : H^2(X, L) \longrightarrow H^2(X_o, L_o) , \] where \(L_o\) is the restriction of \(L\) to \(X_o\). Then we have \[ (5.11.1) \qquad (\varphi^{(2)})^{-1}(H^2(X_o, L_o)') = H^2(X, L)' , \] where the "primes" denote the parts consisting of the neutral elements.
Taking into account 5.5 (iii), this statement is also equivalent to the following:

For every gerbe \(\mathscr{G}\) on \(X\), with band \(L\) as above, denoting by \(\mathscr{G}_o\) the restriction of \(\mathscr{G}\) to \(X_o\), the restriction functor on the categories of sections \[ \mathscr{G}(X) \longrightarrow \mathscr{G}_o(X_o) \] is an equivalence of categories.

The fact that this functor is fully faithful follows indeed from 5.5 (i), and the fact that it is essentially surjective when \(\mathscr{G} \neq \emptyset\) i.e. when the class \(\xi \in H^2(X, L)\) of \(\mathscr{G}\) is neutral, follows from 5.5 (ii). It thus remains to express that \(\mathscr{G}_o(X_o) \neq \emptyset\) implies \(\mathscr{G}(X) \neq \emptyset\), which is none other than (5.11.1).

We shall not give the proof of (5.11.1) here, and we shall content ourselves with pointing out that for every noetherian scheme \(X\) and every subscheme that is closed, one can in fact show that the validity of the statements 5.5 (i) (ii) implies that of (5.11.1); the proof is done rather elementarily, using the descent result VIII 9.4 a).

footnotes.html: (*) The situation has changed since these lines were written, cf. th. 3.1 in M. Artin, Algebraic approximation of structures over complete local rings (to appear).

blocks.html: 6. First reductions
We use the abbreviation \((f,F,g)\) to denote the data of 5.1 in any one of the three cases (i), (ii) or (iii) of this theorem.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1

For 5.1 to be true for the data \((f,F,g)\), where \(f,F\) are fixed, and \(g\) arbitrary, it suffices that for every \(S\)-scheme \(\bar S\), the strict localization of a scheme \(S'\) locally of finite type over \(S\) at a point that is closed in its fibre, the theorem be true for \((\bar f, \bar F, \bar g)\), where \(\bar f, \bar F\) are deduced from \(f, F\) by the base change \(\bar S \to S\), and where \(\bar g : \bar s \to \bar S\) is the inclusion of the closed point of \(\bar S\).

Proof. One may obviously assume \(S,S'\) affine, spectra of rings \(A,A'\). Then \(A'\) is the inductive limit of its sub-\(A\)-algebras of finite type \(A'_i\), and using the theory of passage to the limit (VII 5.11 and 5.14), one is reduced to proving 5.1 for the \((f, F, g_i)\) where \(g_i : \operatorname{Spec}(A'_i) = S'_i \to S\), which brings us back to the case where \(g\) is of finite type. To prove that the base change homomorphisms are isomorphisms, it suffices to prove that they induce isomorphisms on the stalks of the sheaves in play, and it suffices to look at the geometric stalks at points \(s'\) of \(S'\) that are closed in their fibre over \(S\) (VIII 3.13). Let \(\bar s'\) be a geometric point of \(S'\) corresponding to a separable closure of \(k(s')\); since \(s'\) is algebraic over the corresponding point \(s\) of \(S\), \(k(\bar s')\) is therefore also a separable closure of \(k(s)\). Let us denote by \(\bar s\) the prescheme \(\bar s'\), considered as lying over \(S\), i.e. considered as a geometric point of \(S\), and consider the strict localizations \(\bar S\) and \(\bar S'\) of \(S\) at \(\bar s\) and at \(\bar s'\) respectively, so that we have a commutative square. \[ \xymatrix{ \bar s' \ar[r] \ar[d] & \bar s \ar[d] \\ \bar S' \ar[r] & \bar S } \] where the first horizontal arrow is an isomorphism. Taking into account VIII 5.2 and 5.3, the homomorphism induced on the stalks at \(\bar s\) by the homomorphism of base change relative to \((f,F,g)\) is identified with the homomorphism \[ H^i(\bar X, \bar F) \longrightarrow H^i(\bar X', \bar F') \] induced by \(\bar X' \to \bar X\), where \(\bar X\) and \(\bar X'\) denote the schemes deduced from \(X\) by the base changes \(\bar S \to S\) and \(\bar S' \to S\). Now the commutative square above furnishes in an obvious way a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ H^i(\bar X_{\bar s}, \bar F) \ar[r] & H^i(\bar X'_{\bar s}, \bar F') \\ H^i(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r] \ar[u] & H^i(\bar X', \bar F') \ar[u] } \] where the first horizontal arrow is again an isomorphism, hence the second horizontal arrow is an isomorphism as soon as the two vertical arrows are. But this is what the hypothesis of (6.1) ensures, q.e.d.

6.1.1 Thus, to prove 5.1 in a situation \((F,f,-)\), one is reduced to studying the special case 5.5, with \(S\) strictly local. This leads us to study in a general way the situation where one has a morphism \(h : Y \to X\) of schemes, and where one proposes to give the general conditions under which the corresponding homomorphisms \[ H^i(X, F) \longrightarrow H^i(Y, h^*(F)) \] are bijective. The present section will give some easy auxiliary results on this situation, which (for the convenience of later references) we shall state with more generality and precision than would be necessary for the proof of 5.1.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.2

Let \(C,C'\) be two abelian categories, \(T^\bullet = (T^i)\) and \(T'^\bullet = (T'^i)\) two cohomological functors from \(C\) to \(C'\), \(\varphi = (\varphi^i)\) a homomorphism of cohomological functors from \(T^\bullet\) to \(T'^\bullet\). Suppose \(T^\bullet\) and \(T'^\bullet\) are zero in degrees \(< 0\), and \(T^i\) effaceable for \(i > 0\). Let \(n\) be an integer. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a) \(\varphi^i\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n + 1\).
  2. b) (If \(n \geq -1\)). The homomorphism \(\varphi^i\) is a monomorphism if \(i = 0\), and an epimorphism if \(i \leq n\).
  3. c) (If \(n \geq 0\)). The homomorphism \(\varphi^0\) is an isomorphism, and the \(T'^i\) are effaceable for \(0 < i \leq n\).

If these conditions are fulfilled, and if \(A \in \operatorname{Ob}(C)\), then \(\varphi^{n+1}(A) : T^{n+1}(A) \longrightarrow T'^{n+1}(A)\) is an epimorphism (hence an isomorphism) if and only if \(T'^{n+1}(A)\) is effaceable, i.e. if there exists a monomorphism \(A \to B\) such that the corresponding homomorphism \(T'^{n+1}(A) \to T'^{n+1}(B)\) is zero. If \(C' = (\mathrm{Ab})\) (the category of abelian groups), and if \(\xi \in T'^{n+1}(A)\), then \(\xi\) is in the image of \(T^{n+1}(A)\) if and only if \(\xi\) is effaceable, i.e. if there exists a monomorphism \(A \to B\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(T'^{n+1}(B)\) is zero.

Proof. Obviously a) implies b) and c). Since the hypotheses made on \(T^\bullet\) imply that the \(T^i\) \((i > 0)\) are the right satellites of \(T^0\), the implication c) \(\Longrightarrow\) b) follows from the axiomatic characterization of satellite functors; it also follows, by induction on \(n\), from the last assertion of 6.2, which is proved by the well-known argument that we refrain from repeating here (cf. the proof of 6.″ below). The implication b) \(\Longrightarrow\) c) is trivial if \(n = 1\), and if \(n \geq 0\) one proceeds by induction on \(n\): the induction hypothesis allows us to assume that \(\varphi^i\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n-1\), a monomorphism for \(i = n\), hence by hypothesis an isomorphism also for \(i = n\), and it remains to show that it is a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\), using that \(\varphi^n\) is an isomorphism. Let \(A \to B\) be a monomorphism that effaces \(T^{n+1}\), whence an exact sequence \(0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0\) in \(C\), and a homomorphism of exact sequences in \(C'\): \[ \xymatrix{ T^n(B) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^n(C) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{n+1}(A) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{n+1}(B) \ar[d] \\ T'^n(B) \ar[r] & T'^n(C) \ar[r] & T'^{n+1}(A) \ar[r] & T'^{n+1}(B) } \] where the first two vertical arrows are isomorphisms by what we have just seen, and \(T^{n+1}(A) \to T^{n+1}(B)\) is zero by construction. Then the five lemma implies that \(T^{n+1}(A) \to T'^{n+1}(A)\) is a monomorphism, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.3

Suppose that \(T^\bullet, T'^\bullet\) come from cohomological functors (denoted by the same symbols) on the right derived category [3] \(D^+(C)\), with values in \(C'\); one does not necessarily assume the \(T^i\) \((i > 0)\) effaceable. One assumes that \(K^\bullet \in D^+(C)\), \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < 0\) implies \(T^i(K^\bullet) = T'^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < 0\). Let \(K^\bullet \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(C)\) be a complex bounded below in \(C\) such that \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < 0\).

  1. (i) If condition a) of 6.2 is satisfied, then the homomorphism \(\varphi^i(K^\bullet) = T^i(K^\bullet) \to T'^i(K^\bullet)\) is an isomorphism for \(i < n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\).
  2. (ii) Let moreover \(L^\bullet \in \operatorname{Ob} D^+(C)\) be such that \(H^i(L^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < 0\), and let \(u : L^\bullet \to K^\bullet\) be a homomorphism in \(D^+(C)\), inducing an injective homomorphism \(H^0(u) : H^0(L^\bullet) \to H^0(K^\bullet)\). Then, for \(T^{n+1}(L^\bullet) \to T'^{n+1}(L^\bullet)\) to be surjective, it is necessary and sufficient that the image of \(T'^{n+1}(L^\bullet)\) in \(T'^{n+1}(K^\bullet)\) be contained in that of \(T^{n+1}(K^\bullet)\). If \(C' = (\mathrm{Ab})\), and if \(\xi \in T'^{n+1}(L^\bullet)\), then \(\xi\) is in the image of \(T^{n+1}(L^\bullet)\) if and only if its image in \(T'^{n+1}(K^\bullet)\) is in that of \(T^{n+1}(K^\bullet)\).

We recall that the hypothesis that \(T^\bullet\) and \(T'^\bullet\) come from cohomological functors on \(D^+(C)\) can be made explicit by saying that they come from cohomological functors on the abelian category of complexes bounded below of \(C\), commuting with translations of degrees, transforming homomorphisms of complexes homotopic to zero into zero homomorphisms of \(C'\), and transforming every homomorphism \(u : K^\bullet \to L^\bullet\) of complexes that is a quasi-isomorphism (i.e. that induces isomorphisms \(H^i(K^\bullet) \to H^i(L^\bullet)\)) into an isomorphism of \(C'\). In practice, all the cohomological functors from \(C\) to \(C'\) that one encounters are obtained in this way.

Proof of 6.3. Let us first prove (i). The assertion is obvious if \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i \leq n+1\), since then, by the degree properties imposed on \(T^\bullet\), \(T'^\bullet\), we will have \(T^i(K^\bullet) = T'^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i \leq n+1\). Let, on the other hand, \(m\) be an integer \(\geq 0\) such that \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < m\): such an integer exists, e.g. \(m = 0\) works. We proceed by descending induction on \(m\), the assertion being proved when \(m = n+2\). We therefore assume the assertion proved for the \(m' > m\), and prove it for \(m\). By the hypothesis on the degrees of \(K^\bullet\), \(K^\bullet\) is quasi-isomorphic to a complex in degrees \(\geq m\), so we may assume it to be in degrees \(\geq m\). There follows an exact sequence of complexes \[ 0 \longrightarrow H^m [-m] \longrightarrow K^\bullet \longrightarrow K'^\bullet \longrightarrow 0 , \] where \(H^m = H^m(K^\bullet)\), where the sign \([-m]\) indicates a shift by \(-m\) on the degrees of a complex, and where \(K'^\bullet\) is defined as the cokernel. Hence the cohomology objects of \(K'^\bullet\) are those of \(K^\bullet\) in degrees \(\geq m+1\), and are zero in degrees \(\leq m+1\); in particular, we may apply the induction hypothesis to \(K'^\bullet\). The preceding exact sequence gives rise to a homomorphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ T^{i-1}(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{i-m}(H^m) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^i(K^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^i(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{i+1-m}(H^m) \ar[d] \\ T'^{i-1}(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{i-m}(H^m) \ar[r] & T'^i(K^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^i(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{i+1-m}(H^m) } \] Then, taking \(i \leq n\) in the preceding diagram, and taking into account the induction hypothesis and \(m \geq 0\), we find that the vertical arrows around the middle vertical arrow are isomorphisms and a fortiori epimorphisms, and that the right-hand vertical arrow is a monomorphism, so by the five lemma the middle vertical arrow is an epimorphism. Taking \(i \leq n+1\), we find likewise that the vertical arrows around the middle one are monomorphisms, the left-hand vertical arrow being an isomorphism and a fortiori an epimorphism, whence we conclude by the five lemma that the middle vertical arrow is a monomorphism, which establishes 6.3 (i).

To establish the second assertion 6.3 (ii), one uses likewise the exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow L^\bullet \longrightarrow K^\bullet \longrightarrow K'^\bullet \longrightarrow 0 , \] where \(K^\bullet\) is defined as the mapping-cylinder of \(L^\bullet \to K^\bullet\), and so still has cohomology in positive degrees. The usual "diagram chase" in \[ \xymatrix{ T^n(K^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^n(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{n+1}(L^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{n+1}(K^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{n+1}(K'^\bullet) \ar[d] \\ T'^n(K^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^n(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{n+1}(L^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{n+1}(K^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{n+1}(K'^\bullet) } \] then yields the last assertion of 6.3, taking into account the fact that (by the first part already proved) the first two vertical arrows are isomorphisms, and the last two monomorphisms. This completes the proof of 6.3.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.4

Theorem (5.1) is true if \(f\) is finite.
This indeed follows at once from VIII 5.5 and 5.8.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5

Let \(h : Y \to X\) be a morphism of quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes. In (i) below, \(I\) denotes a given set having at least two points; in (ii) and (iii), \(\mathbb{L}\) denotes a non-empty subset of the set \(\mathbb{P}\) of prime numbers, and in (iii) \(n\) denotes an integer.

(i) The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a) For every sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(X\), the canonical map \[ H^0(X,F) \longrightarrow H^0(Y,h^*(F)) \] is injective (resp. bijective).
  2. b) For every finite morphism \(X' \to X\), denoting by \(h' : Y' \to X'\) the morphism deduced from \(h\) by the base change \(X' \to X\), the canonical map \[ H^0(X', I_{X'}) \longrightarrow H^0(Y', I_{Y'}) \] deduced from \(h'\) is injective (resp. bijective).
  3. b') With the notation of b), the map \(U \mapsto h'^{-1}(U)\) from the set of subsets of \(Y'\) that are both open and closed to the set of subsets of \(X'\) that are both open and closed is injective (resp. bijective).
  4. b'') (If \(X\) locally noetherian). With the notation of b), the map induced on the sets of connected components \[ \pi_0(h') : \pi_0(Y') \longrightarrow \pi_0(X') \] is surjective (resp. bijective); or again: if \(X'\) is non-empty (resp. connected non-empty) then so is \(Y'\).

Moreover, if these conditions are satisfied, then for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the functor \(P \mapsto h^*(P)\) from the category of torsors (= principal homogeneous bundles) under \(F\) to the category of torsors under \(h^*(F)\) is faithful (resp. fully faithful), and a fortiori, in the "resp." case, the canonical map \[ H^1(X,F) \longrightarrow H^1(Y,h^*(F)) \] is injective. Finally, under the same hypotheses, the functor \(X' \mapsto Y' = X' \times_X Y\) from the category of étale coverings of \(X\) to the category of étale coverings of \(Y\) is faithful (resp. fully faithful).

(ii) The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a) For every sheaf \(F\) of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-finite groups on \(X\), the canonical map \[ H^i(X,F) \longrightarrow H^i(Y,h^*(F)) \] is bijective for \(i = 0,1\).
  2. b) For every finite morphism \(X' \to X\), denoting by \(h' : Y' \to X'\) the morphism deduced from \(h\) by base change, and for every finite ordinary \(\mathbb{L}\)-group \(G\), the canonical map \[ H^i(X', G_{X'}) \longrightarrow H^i(Y', G_{Y'}) \] is bijective for \(i = 0,1\).
  3. b') (If \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)). With the notation of b), the inverse image functor by \(h'\) induces an equivalence between the category of étale coverings of \(X'\) and the category of étale coverings of \(Y'\).
  4. b'') (If \(X\) noetherian, \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)). With the notation of b), if \(X'\) is non-empty, then so is \(Y'\), and if \(y'\) is a geometric point of \(Y'\), \(x'\) its image in \(X'\), the canonical map \[ \pi_i(Y',y') \longrightarrow \pi_i(X',x') , \quad \text{for } i = 0,1 , \] is bijective.

(iii) The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a) For every sheaf \(F\) of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(X\), the homomorphism \[ H^i(X,F) \longrightarrow H^i(Y,h^*(F)) \] is an isomorphism if \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism if \(i = n+1\).
  2. a') (If \(n \geq -1\)). For every \(F\) as above, the homomorphism in question is injective if \(i = 0\), and surjective if \(i \leq n\).
  3. b) (If \(n \geq -1\)). For every finite morphism \(X' \to X\), denoting by \(h' : Y' \to X'\) the morphism deduced from \(h\) by the base change \(X' \to X\), and for every \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\), \(\nu > 0\), the canonical homomorphism \[ H^i(X', (\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z})_{X'}) \longrightarrow H^i(Y', (\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z})_{Y'}) \] is injective for \(i = 0\), surjective for \(i \leq n\).
Moreover, we have the following complement to the preceding statement:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6

(i) Suppose the non-"resp." condition 6.5 (i) a) satisfied, let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets on \(X\), and let \(\xi \in H^0(Y,h^*(F))\). Suppose that there exists a monomorphism of sheaves of sets \(F \to G\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(H^0(Y,h^*(G))\) lies in the image of \(H^0(X,G)\). Then \(\xi\) lies in the image of \(H^0(X,F)\).

(ii) Suppose the "resp." condition 6.5 (i) a) satisfied, let \(F\) be a sheaf of groups on \(X\), and let \(\xi \in H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). Suppose that there exists a monomorphism of sheaves of groups \(F \to G\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(H^1(Y,h^*(G))\) lies in the image of \(H^1(X,G)\); then \(\xi\) lies in the image of \(H^1(X,F)\).

(iii) Suppose the condition 6.5 (iii) a) satisfied (for a given value \(n\)), let \(F\) be a sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(X\) and let \(\xi \in H^{n+1}(Y,h^*(F))\). Suppose that there exists a monomorphism \(F \to G\) of sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion, such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(H^{n+1}(Y,h^*(G))\) lies in the image of \(H^{n+1}(X,G)\); then \(\xi\) lies in the image of \(H^{n+1}(X,F)\).

Proof of 6.5 and 6.6. Let us first prove 6.6. The case of 6.6 (iii) is a special case of the last assertion in 6.3, applied to the case where \(C\) is the category of abelian sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(X\), \(C'\) is the category (Ab), and \(T^i(F) = H^i(X,F)\), \(T'^i(F) = H^i(Y,h^*(F))\) (note that \(T'^\bullet\) is indeed a cohomological functor in \(F\), thanks to the fact that the functor \(h^*\) is exact). Of course, here the consideration of complexes as in 6.3 is unnecessary (it will be convenient for us later on (6.8)) and we use solely the last assertion of 6.3.

To prove (i), consider the amalgamated sum \(H = G \amalg_F G\), the inductive limit, in the category of sheaves of sets on \(X\), of the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r] \ar[dr] & G \\ & G } \] The usual exactness properties of the topos of sheaves of sets show, since \(F \to G\) is a monomorphism, that we have an exact diagram of sheaves of sets on \(X\) \[ F \longrightarrow G \rightrightarrows H \] (which can be expressed by saying that in a topos, every monomorphism is effective, and proved by reducing as usual to the category of sets). Since the functors \(H^0\) and \(h^*\) are left exact, we deduce a homomorphism of exact diagrams of sets \[ \xymatrix{ H^0(X,F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^0(X,G) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] \ar[d] & H^0(X,H) \ar[d] \\ H^0(Y,h^*(F)) \ar[r] & H^0(Y,h^*(G)) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & H^0(Y,h^*(H)) } \] where the vertical arrows are injective. An immediate "diagram chase" then proves the assertion 6.6 (i).

To prove 6.6 (ii), we shall first prove the second assertion of 6.5 (i), namely that, granting condition a) of 6.5 (i), for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the functor \(P \mapsto h^*(P)\), from the category of torsors under \(F\) to the category of torsors under \(h^*(F)\), is faithful (resp. fully faithful), and hence, in the "resp." case, induces an injection on the \(H^1\). For this, if \(P\) and \(P'\) are two torsors under \(F\), let us denote by \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P')\) the sheaf of \(F\)-isomorphisms from \(P\) onto \(P'\). It is immediate that the formation of this sheaf commutes with every extension of the base, in particular with the extension of the base by \(h\). (This is an assertion valid for every morphism of sites). Using the hypothesis on the effect of \(h^*\) on the \(H^0\) for the sheaf \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P')\), we find that the map \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P') \to \underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(h^*(P),h^*(P'))\) is injective (resp. bijective), which means that the functor \(P \mapsto h^*(P)\) is faithful (resp. fully faithful). (NB: in the category of torsors under a sheaf of groups, every homomorphism is an isomorphism). Let us note on the other hand that if \(F\) is a subsheaf of groups of a sheaf of groups \(G\), then giving a torsor \(P\) under \(F\) amounts to giving a torsor under \(G\) (namely the one deduced from \(P\) by extension \(F \to G\) of the structural Group), equipped with a section of \(Q/F\) (which is indeed interpreted as a "restriction of the structural Group" from \(G\) to \(F\)). This being said, with the notation of 6.6 (ii), since the image \(\eta\) of \(\xi\) in \(H^1(Y,h^*(G))\) comes from an element of \(H^1(X,G)\), the latter is defined by a torsor \(Q\) under \(G\), so that \(\eta\) is the class of the torsor \(h^*(Q)\) under \(h^*(G)\). The fact that \(\eta\) comes from a \(\xi \in H^1(Y,h^*(F))\) then makes explicit by saying that \(\xi\) is the class of the \(h^*(F)\)-torsor defined by \(h^*(Q)\) and a suitable section of \(h^*(Q)/h^*(F)\). Since the functor \(h^*\) is right exact, this last sheaf is none other than \(h^*(Q/F)\), and since \(h^*\) induces a bijection on the \(H^0\) of sheaves of sets, it follows that the section in question of \(h^*(Q)/h^*(F)\) comes from a section of \(Q/F\). This last then defines an \(F\)-torsor by restriction of the structural group, and the class of this torsor in \(H^1(X,F)\) evidently has \(\xi\) as image in \(H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). This proves 6.6 (ii) and completes the proof of 6.6.

Let us now prove 6.5, beginning with 6.5 (iii). Evidently a) implies a'), and the reverse implication is a special case of 6.2 (applied again to the case where \(C\) is the category of sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(X\), and \(C'\) the category of sheaves of abelian groups), provided one proves the effaceability in \(C\) of the functors \(H^i(X,F)\) for \(i > 0\). This indeed offers no difficulty, but we can also dispense with proving this result, by noting that \(F\) is the filtered inductive limit of its subsheaves \(F_i\) for which there exists an integer \(n > 0\) annihilating \(F_i\) (IX 1.1). Then \(h^*(F)\) is the inductive limit of the \(h^*(F_i)\), and taking into account the commutation of cohomology with inductive limits (VII 3.3), resulting from the hypotheses of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation made on \(X\) and \(Y\) (which had not been used for 6.6), we reduce to proving condition a) for the \(F_i\), which brings us to the case where there exists an integer \(m > 0\) such that \(mF = 0\). We may evidently assume that the prime divisors of \(m\) are \(\in \mathbb{L}\), and we may then take for \(C\) the category of sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\)-Modules on \(X\). But it is known that in this category, the functors \(H^i(X, - )\) for \(i \geq 1\) are effaceable ( ). This shows the equivalence of the conditions a) and a') of 6.5 (iii). On the other hand, applying a) to the direct image of a sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(F'\) on \(X'\), \(X'\) finite over \(X\), which is \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion thanks to IX 1.2 (v), 1.6 (iii), and using 6.4 and VIII 5.5, we find that the homomorphism \[ H^i(X',F') \longrightarrow H^i(Y',h'^*(F')) \] is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\), whence a fortiori condition b). It remains to prove that this condition implies a'). For this, let us use the fact (IX 2.7.2) that every sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(F\) on \(X\) is the filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion; then the argument of passage to the limit already used shows that in a'), one may restrict to the case where \(F\) is constructible. By virtue of IX 2.14 there then exist a finite number of finite morphisms \(p_i : X'_i \to X\), constant sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(G_{X'_i}\) on the \(X'_i\), and an injective homomorphism \[ F \longrightarrow \prod_i p_{i*}(G_{X'_i}) \] This said, if \(n = -1\), i.e. when the desired conclusion reduces to the injectivity assertion for \(H^0(X,F) \to H^0(Y,h^*(F))\), one sees at once that in this question one may replace \(F\) by a sheaf \(G\) such that there exists a monomorphism \(F \to G\), and consequently one may replace \(F\) by the product of the \(p_{i*}(G_{X'_i})\). Taking 6.4 into account, we are thus reduced to proving the assertion by replacing \(h : Y \to X\) by \(h' : Y' \to X'\), and \(F\) by a constant sheaf on \(X'\) with value a finite ordinary group of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(G\). But \(G\) is isomorphic to a sum of groups of the form \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}\), with \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\). We are thus indeed reduced to verifying b). When \(n \geq 0\), one proceeds analogously. By induction on \(n\), we may assume the desired conclusion (and consequently a)) proved for the integer \(n-1\) instead of \(n\). Then using 6.6 (iii), one sees that one may again replace \(F\) by a sheaf \(G\) such that there exists a monomorphism \(F \to G\), and one will again take for \(G\) the sheaf \(p_*(G_{X'})\). Taking 6.4 into account and the vanishing of the \(R^i p_*\) \((i \geq 1)\) for a finite morphism (VIII 5.5), this brings us again to proving surjectivity for \(H^n\) by replacing \(h : Y \to X\) by an \(h' : Y' \to X'\), and \(F\) by a constant sheaf on \(X'\) with value a finite ordinary group of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion. Since injectivity is already secured thanks to the induction hypothesis and the implication a') \(\Longrightarrow\) a), we are again reduced, by dévissage on \(G\), to the case where \(G\) is of the form \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}\), that is, to the case considered in condition b) of 6.5 (iii). This proves case (iii) of 6.5.

Cases (i) and (ii) are proved in exactly the same way, as far as the equivalence of the conditions a) and b) in 6.5 (i) resp. 6.5 (ii) is concerned: one uses IX 2.7.2 and the commutation of \(H^0\) and \(H^1\) with filtered inductive limits of sheaves (VII 5.14) to reduce to the case where \(F\) is constructible, then IX 2.14, 6.6 (i)(ii) and VIII 5.8 to reduce to the special case considered in b). Furthermore, in (i), the equivalence of the conditions b), b') and b'') is trivial and is stated only for the record, as is the fact that they imply the faithfulness (resp. full faithfulness) of the functor \(X' \mapsto Y'\) from the category of étale coverings of \(X\) to the category of étale coverings of \(Y\). The same holds for the equivalence of the conditions b), b') and b'') in 6.5 (ii), which were added for good measure. The proof of 6.5 is thus complete.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.7

(*) 1) Evidently, the arguments proving 6.5 and 6.6 are of a very general and essentially trivial nature, and it would be worthwhile to isolate them as abstract lemmas of the same water as 6.2 (the sheaves \(p_*(G_{X'})\) playing the role of cogenerators of the category \(C\) in which one works). We leave this pleasant exercise to the reader, and we merely point out that essentially the same statement could be given by looking at functors such as \(R^i f_*\) instead of the functors \(H^i\). The same remarks apply to 6.8, 6.11 below.

2) When \(X\) is noetherian, the arguments given show that in the statement of conditions b) and their variants in 6.5 (i) (ii) (iii), one may restrict oneself to taking \(X'\) integral; when \(X\) is universally Japanese, one may even take them integral and normal; this is also possible without the Japanese restriction on \(X\), provided one takes morphisms \(p : X' \to X\) that are integral instead of finite morphisms. We shall not make use of any of these variants in the remainder of the seminar.

3) The proof of 6.6 does not use the hypothesis of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation made on \(X\), and the same holds for the fact that in (i) (ii) (iii) condition a) implies the others, as well as for the equivalence of the conditions b), b'), b'') among themselves. Let us note on the other hand that form b) of the conditions 6.5 (i) shows that, for \(\mathbb{L} = \emptyset\), they are special cases (when \(X\) is quasi-compact quasi-separated) of 6.5 (iii), for \(n = -1\) resp. for \(n = 0\). This moreover remains true (restricting to the conditions in form a)) without the restriction stated on \(X\), as one sees easily thanks to the fact that for every sheaf of sets \(F\), and every prime number \(\ell\), one can find two abelian sheaves of \(\ell\)-torsion \(G\) and \(H\), and a homomorphism \(u : G \to H\) of the underlying sheaves of sets, such that \(F\) is isomorphic to the inverse image of the zero section (one will take for \(G\) the free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}\)-Module generated by \(F\), and for \(H\) the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}\) on \(X\)). The same argument shows that (without any restriction of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation) 6.5 (ii) a) (where it even suffices to take \(i = 0\)) implies the "resp." condition 6.5(i) a); this in turn allows, taking into account that this last already implies the injectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\) for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), to restrict oneself in the statement of 6.5 (ii) a) to requiring for \(i = 1\) the surjectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). Unfortunately, the case 6.5 (ii) cannot be viewed as a special case of 6.5 (iii), which often obliges us to repeat in the non-commutative case an argument already made essentially in the commutative case. Let us also note that, except for 6.10, the results that follow are stated so as to be valid without any hypothesis of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.8

(Descent lemma). With the general notation of 6.5, suppose given in addition a morphism \(p : \bar X \to X\), let us denote by \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) the morphism deduced from \(h\) by the base change \(p\), and by \(p_Y : \bar Y \to Y\) the canonical morphism. We assume either that \(p\) is surjective, or that \(h\) is a closed immersion and that \(X = p(\bar X) \cup h(Y)\).

(i) Suppose that the morphism \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the injectivity (resp. bijectivity) condition of 6.5 (i) a). In the "resp." case, suppose in addition that the base change morphism \[ (*) \qquad h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) \] is injective for every sheaf of sets \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\). Then the morphism \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the injectivity (resp. bijectivity) condition of 6.5 (i) a).

(ii) Suppose that \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the condition of 6.5 (ii) a), and that for every sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change morphism (*) is bijective. Then \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the condition of 6.5 (ii) a).

(iii) Suppose that \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the condition of 6.5 (iii) a), and that for every abelian sheaf \(\bar F\) of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism \[ h^*(R^i p_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) \] is bijective for \(i \leq n-1\), injective for \(i = n\) (where \(n\) is a given integer \(\geq 1\)). Then the morphism \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the condition of 6.5 (iii) a).

Proof of 6.8. In the case where \(p\) is not assumed surjective, but \(h\) is a closed immersion and \(X = p(\bar X) \cup h(Y)\), we consider the sum scheme \(\bar X'\) of \(\bar X\) and \(Y\), and the morphism \(p' : \bar X' \to X\) deduced from \(p\) and \(h\). Then \(p'\) is surjective; moreover one verifies trivially, in each of the three cases considered (i) (ii) (iii), that the hypotheses made on the pair \((h,p)\) are still satisfied for the pair \((h,p')\). This therefore brings us to the case where \(p\) is surjective, in which we shall place ourselves in what follows. In this case, for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the canonical homomorphism \[ F \longrightarrow p_*(p^*(F)) \] is injective. In case (i), to verify the injectivity of \(H^0(X,F) \to H^0(Y,h^*(F))\), we are reduced at once to the case where we replace \(F\) by \(p_*(\bar F)\) (where we set \(\bar F = p^*(F)\)). Now consider the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ H^0(X, p_*(\bar F)) \ar[r] \ar[dd]_{\wr} & H^0(Y, h^*(p_*(\bar F))) \ar[d] \\ & H^0(Y, p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ H^0(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r] & H^0(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F)) , } \] where the left-hand vertical arrow and the second right-hand vertical arrow are the canonical isomorphisms, the first right-hand vertical arrow coming from the base change homomorphism by \(h\). By hypothesis the second horizontal arrow is injective, which immediately implies that the same holds for the first, which proves the non-"resp." assertion of (i). For the "resp." assertion, one assumes that the second horizontal arrow is surjective; moreover, the base change homomorphism being a monomorphism by hypothesis, the same holds for the first right-hand vertical arrow, hence for the composite of the two right-hand vertical arrows. It follows at once that the first horizontal arrow is also surjective, which completes the proof of (i). To prove (ii), thanks to what precedes and 6.5 (i) we are reduced to proving the surjectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). Using 6.6 (ii) we are again reduced to proving it for \(F\) of the form \(p_*(\bar F)\), where \(\bar F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups on \(\bar X\) (IX 1.6 (ii)). Writing the exact sequences for the \(H^1\), (variants of (3.2)) for the morphisms \(p\) and \(p_Y\), we find a homomorphism of non-commutative exact sequences: \[ \xymatrix{ H^1(X, p_*(\bar F)) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^0(X, R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \ar[d] \\ H^1(Y, p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) \ar[r] & H^1(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F)) \ar[r] & H^0(Y, R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) , } \] where in each row the first arrow is injective and identifies the first term with the inverse image, by the second arrow, of the marked point of the third term. By hypothesis on \(\bar h\), the middle vertical arrow is bijective. On the other hand, the two extreme vertical arrows factor respectively through \(H^1(Y,h^*(p_*(\bar F)))\) and \(H^0(Y,h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)))\), by composing the homomorphisms \(H^i(X,-) \to H^i(Y,-)\) (for \(i = 1\) and \(i = 0\) respectively) and the homomorphisms deduced by applying \(H^i(Y,-)\) (for these same values of \(i\)) to the base change homomorphism \(h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \to p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) resp. \(h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \to R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\). Since the first of these arrows is an isomorphism by hypothesis, it follows that the first vertical arrow of the diagram above is identified with the homomorphism \(H^1(X,-) \to H^1(Y,-)\) that we wish to study. To prove its bijectivity, it therefore remains to prove that the last vertical arrow of the diagram is injective. Now, by what we have just said, it is composed of two maps, of which the first is a canonical homomorphism \(H^0(X,-) \to H^0(Y,-)\), hence bijective, and the second is injective, since deduced by the left exact functor \(H^0(Y,-)\) from a homomorphism \(h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \to R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) which is a monomorphism. This last fact indeed follows easily from the bijectivity hypothesis made for the homomorphism of base change in the preceding dimension \(0\), for example by using the second assertion of 6.5 (i) and the usual computation of the stalks of the higher direct images (VIII 5.3). This proves 6.8 (ii).

It remains to prove 6.8 (iii). For this, it will be more convenient for us, instead of using directly the injection \(F \to p_*(p^*(F))\) as above, to use the homomorphism \[ F \longrightarrow Rp_*(\bar F) \] in the right derived category \(D^+(C)\), where \(C\) denotes the category of abelian sheaves on \(X\). Let us recall that by definition, \(Rp_*(\bar F)\) is the complex \(p_*(C(\bar F))\), where \(C(\bar F)\) is an injective resolution complex of \(\bar F\) in the category of abelian sheaves on \(\bar X\). If \(K^\bullet\) is a complex on \(X\), we denote by \(H^i(X,K^\bullet)\) the hypercohomology groups of \(X\) with coefficients in \(K^\bullet\), and one uses the analogous notation on \(Y\). By virtue of 6.3, we are reduced to proving the surjectivity for \[ (1) \qquad H^n(X, Rp_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow H^n(Y, h^* Rp_*(\bar F)) \] Now by hypothesis, the base change homomorphism \[ (2) \qquad h^*(Rp_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow Rp_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) \] induces an isomorphism on the cohomology sheaves in degrees \(\leq n-1\), and a monomorphism in degrees \(n\), which can be expressed by saying that the "mapping-cylinder" \(K^\bullet\) of the preceding homomorphism has non-zero cohomology sheaves only in degrees \(\geq n\). Hence \(H^i(Y,K^\bullet) = 0\) if \(i < n\), which implies, by the exact cohomology sequence, that the homomorphisms \[ (3) \qquad H^i(Y, h^*(Rp_*(\bar F))) \longrightarrow H^i(Y, Rp_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) \] induced by the above homomorphism, are isomorphisms for \(i \leq n-1\), a monomorphism for \(i = n\). Consider the composite of (1) and (3) \[ (4) \qquad H^n(X, Rp_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow H^n(Y, h^*(Rp_*(\bar F))) \longrightarrow H^n(Y, Rp_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) . \] The extreme terms are respectively isomorphic, by virtue of the definitions, to \(H^n(\bar X, \bar F)\) and \(H^n(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F))\), and the composite of (4) is none other than the homomorphism deduced from \(\bar h\), which is itself bijective thanks to the hypothesis made on \(\bar h\). Since the second arrow of (4) is injective by what we have just seen, the first is likewise bijective, which completes the proof of 6.8.
Moreover, one observes at once that the preceding proof yields the following result, slightly more precise and more general:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.9

The notation is that of 6.8. Suppose in addition that the non-"resp." condition of 6.5 (i) is satisfied for \(h\) (resp. the "resp." condition of 6.5 (i), resp. the condition of 6.5 (iii), with \(n \geq -1\)), and that for every sheaf of sets \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism \(h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \to p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) is injective (resp. bijective, resp. that for every sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism \(h^* R^i p_*(\bar F) \to R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) is bijective for \(i \leq n\), injective for \(i = n+1\)). Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. a sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) on \(X\), and let \(\xi \in H^{n+1}(Y,h^*(F))\) (where one takes \(n = -1\) in the case (i), \(n = 0\) in case (ii)). Set \(\bar F = p^*(F)\). Then, in order for \(\xi\) to lie in the image of \(H^{n+1}(X,F)\), it is necessary and sufficient that its inverse image in \(H^{n+1}(\bar Y, p_Y^*(h^*(F))) = H^{n+1}(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F))\) lie in the image of \(H^{n+1}(\bar X, \bar F)\).
We shall use this refined form of 6.8 to prove the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.10

The notation is that of 6.5. We assume, for simplicity, that the non-"resp." condition of 6.5 (i) is verified.

(i) In order for the "resp." condition of 6.5 (i) to be satisfied (resp. for 6.5 (ii) a) to hold, resp. for 6.5 (iii) a) to hold), it is necessary and sufficient that the following condition be satisfied: For every sheaf \(F\) of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian groups of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) on \(X\), every \(\xi \in H^0(Y,h^*(F))\) (resp. every \(\xi \in H^i(Y,h^*(F))\) with \(i = 0,1\), resp. every \(\xi \in H^i(Y,h^*(F))\) with \(i \leq n\)), and every non-empty closed subset \(X'\) of \(X\), denoting by \(Y'\) its inverse image in \(Y\), there exists a morphism \(p : \bar X \to X\) satisfying the following conditions:

  1. 1°) The image \(p(\bar X)\) is contained in \(X'\) and contains a non-empty open subset of \(X'\).
  2. 2°) For every sheaf of sets \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\) (resp....) the base change homomorphism \(h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \to p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) is an isomorphism (resp. for every sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups \(\bar F\) on \(X\), the base change homomorphism \(h^*(R^i p_*(\bar F)) \to R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) for \(i = 0,1\) is bijective, resp. for every abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism is bijective for \(i \leq n\)).
  3. 3°) The inverse image of \(\xi\) in \(H^i(\bar Y, p_Y^*(h^*(F))) = H^i(\bar Y, \bar h^*(p^*(F)))\) is contained in the image of \(H^i(\bar X, p^*(F))\).

(ii) Let \(n \geq -1\), and suppose that for every sheaf of sets \(F\) (resp. every sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. every abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) \(F\) on \(X\), the homomorphism \(H^i(X,F) \to H^i(Y,h^*(F))\) is bijective for \(i \leq n\), injective for \(i = n+1\), (in the first case, one assumes \(n = -1\); in the second, \(n = -1\) or \(0\)). Let \(\xi \in H^{n+1}(Y,h^*(F))\). In order for \(\xi\) to lie in the image of \(H^{n+1}(X,F)\), it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the condition stated in (i) above, with \(i = n+1\).
Proof of 6.10. Using 6.5 and an immediate induction on \(n\), one observes that 6.10 (i) is a consequence of 6.10 (ii), which we shall now prove.

Suppose that \(\xi\) does not lie in the image of \(H^n(X,F)\). Let \(\Phi\) be the set of closed subsets \(X'\) of \(X\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(H^n(Y', h^*(F)|Y')\) is not contained in that of \(H^n(X', F|X')\). By hypothesis, \(X \in \Phi\), so \(\Phi\) is non-empty. Order \(\Phi\) by the relation \(\supset\), and let us show that \(\Phi\) is inductive. For this, it suffices to prove that if \((X'_\lambda)\) is a totally ordered family of elements of \(\Phi\), and if \(X'\) is their intersection, then \(X' \in \Phi\). Now, equipping the \(X'_\lambda\) and \(X'\) with the reduced induced structure, one sees that the morphisms \(X'_\lambda \to X\) are affine (since they are closed immersions), so the projective system of the \(X'_\lambda\) satisfies the conditions considered in VII 5. Moreover, one observes at once that \(X'\) is the projective limit of the \(X'_\lambda\). Likewise, \(Y'\) is the projective limit of the projective system of the \(Y'_\lambda\), which are affine over \(Y\). Using VII 5.8, we therefore find \[ \varinjlim H^n(X'_\lambda, F|X'_\lambda) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(X', F|X') , \quad \varinjlim H^n(Y'_\lambda, h^*(F)|Y'_\lambda) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(Y', h^*(F)|Y') . \] From this, one concludes at once that if one had \((\xi|Y') \in \operatorname{Im} H^n(X', F|X')\), then there would exist an index \(\lambda\) such that \((\xi|Y'_\lambda) \in \operatorname{Im} H^n(X'_\lambda, F|X'_\lambda)\), which is absurd; so one indeed has \(X' \in \Phi\). Hence \(\Phi\) is inductive, and consequently contains a minimal element, say \(X'\). Since evidently \(\emptyset \notin \Phi\), \(X'\) is non-empty. Let us apply to \(\xi\) and to \(X'\) the hypothesis of 6.10, whence a morphism \(p : \bar X \to X\) satisfying conditions 1°) to 3°) stated in 6.10. Note that one may even assume \(p\) surjective. Indeed, let \(U\) be a non-empty open subset of \(X'\) contained in \(p(\bar X)\), and let \(X'_1\) be its complement in \(X'\), so that by construction one has \(X'_1 \notin \Phi\). Using this relation, one sees at once that, setting \(\bar X_1 = \bar X \amalg X'_1\) and denoting by \(p_1 : \bar X_1 \to X\) the morphism defined by \(p\) and the inclusion of \(X'_1\) into \(X\), the morphism \(p_1\) still satisfies the same hypotheses as \(p\); moreover, it is surjective. We therefore assume \(p\) surjective, and now apply 6.9, replacing therein the morphism \(h : Y \to X\) by the morphism \(h' : Y' \to X'\) (\(X'\) being equipped, say, with the reduced induced structure), and \(\xi\) by \(\xi|Y'\). One then concludes from 6.9 that one has \((\xi|Y') \in \operatorname{Im} H^n(X', F|X')\), which contradicts the relation \(X' \in \Phi\) and completes the proof of 6.10.

We shall use 6.10 to reduce 5.5 to the case where \(f\) is a projective morphism; but for this, in the non-noetherian case, we shall need a non-noetherian variant of Chow's lemma, which will be given in the following number.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.11

(Transitivity lemma). The notation is that of 6.8, but no surjectivity hypothesis is made relative to \(p\). We assume that \(h\) satisfies condition (i) a) (resp. (ii) a), resp. (iii) a) of 6.5. We assume moreover, in case (i), that for every sheaf of sets \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism of 6.8 is a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism); in case (ii), that \(\bar X\) is noetherian and that for every sheaf \(\bar F\) of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, the base change homomorphism \(h^*(R^i p_*(\bar F)) \to R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) is bijective for \(i = 0,1\); finally, in the case (iii), that the base change homomorphism is bijective for \(i \leq n\), injective for \(i = n+1\). Then the morphism \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) also satisfies condition (i) (resp. (ii), resp. (iii)) of 6.5.

Proof of 6.11. In case (i), one considers the commutative diagram of the proof of 6.8 (i). Here the hypotheses imply that the first horizontal arrow and the first right-hand vertical arrow are injective (resp. bijective), so the same holds for the second horizontal arrow, which is what we wanted to establish. In case (ii), one is given a sheaf \(\bar F\) of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups on \(\bar X\), and one must show that every element of \(H^1(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F))\) comes from an element of \(H^1(\bar X, \bar F)\). By virtue of 6.6 (ii) applied to \(\bar h\), it suffices to find a monomorphism \(\bar F \to \bar G\) of sheaves of groups on \(\bar X\) that effaces \(H^1(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F))\). Now consider the second row of the diagram used in the proof of 6.8 (ii). It suffices successively to find a monomorphism \(\bar F \to \bar G\), with \(\bar G\) a sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-finite groups, that effaces the last term \(H^0(Y, R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)))\), then a monomorphism of sheaves of groups \(\bar G \to \bar H\) that effaces \(H^1(Y, p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)))\). Now, as we remarked in the proof of 6.8 (i), the two terms to be effaced are isomorphic respectively, by the extreme vertical arrows of the diagram in question, to \(H^0(X, R^1 p_*(\bar F))\) and to \(H^1(X, p_*(\bar F))\), taking into account the hypothesis on the homomorphisms of base change made here on \(p,h\). Moreover, the isomorphisms in question are evidently functorial in \(\bar F\), so that it suffices to efface the two preceding terms. Now by virtue of 3.3 one may efface \(R^1 p_*(\bar F)\) (and a fortiori \(H^0(X, R^1 p_*(\bar F))\)) by a monomorphism of \(\bar F\) into an ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-group \(\bar G\). It remains to efface \(H^1(X, p_*(\bar F))\), which is possible thanks to the fact that by the diagram in question, this last term maps into \(H^1(\bar X, \bar F)\) by a monomorphism functorial in \(\bar F\), and that \(H^1(\bar X, \bar F)\) is again effaceable thanks to 3.3.

It remains to treat case (iii), and for this one too we take up in reverse the proof of 6.8 (*). One must prove that the homomorphism \[ H^i(\bar X, \bar F) \longrightarrow H^i(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F)) \] is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), and a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\). Now the preceding homomorphisms are induced by a homomorphism of complexes \[ \mathbb{R}\Gamma_{\bar X}(\bar F) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\Gamma_{\bar Y}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) , \] deduced from an injective resolution \(C(\bar F)\) and a homomorphism from \(\bar h^*(C(\bar F))\) (which is a resolution of \(\bar h^*(\bar F)\)) into an injective resolution of \(\bar h^*(\bar F)\). The above homomorphism is also identified with the composite homomorphism \[ \mathbb{R}\Gamma_X(Rp_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\Gamma_Y(h^*(Rp_*(\bar F))) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\Gamma_Y(Rp_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) , \] where the first homomorphism is the homomorphism \(h^*\) relative to \(Rp_*(\bar F)\), and the second is deduced from the base change homomorphisms \(h^*(Rp_*(\bar F)) \to Rp_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) by applying \(\mathbb{R}\Gamma_Y\). The first homomorphism therefore induces an isomorphism on the cohomology groups of the complexes in question, by virtue of the hypothesis made on \(h\) and of 6.3 (i). The same holds for the second, by virtue of the hypothesis we have made on the base change homomorphisms, using the argument given in the proof of 6.8 (iii). Consequently, the same conclusion applies to the composite of the two, which completes the proof of 6.11.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.12

The argument given for 6.11 in cases (i) and (iii) yields an even more precise result: in order to be able to conclude, for a given sheaf \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), that \(H^i(\bar X, \bar F) \to H^i(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F))\) is bijective for \(i \leq n\), injective for \(i = n+1\), it suffices to assume

1°) the base change homomorphism \(h^*(R^i p_*(\bar F)) \to R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\), and

2°) for every pair of integers \(i,j \geq 0\), the homomorphism \(H^i(X, R^j p_*(\bar F)) \to H^i(Y, h^*(R^j p_*(\bar F)))\) induced by \(h\) is an isomorphism if \(i+j \leq n\), a monomorphism if \(i+j = n+1\).

It is plausible that one has an analogous result in case (ii), but its statement would necessarily have to involve non-commutative 2-cohomology. It is to avoid recourse to this theory that we have used a different argument in 6.10 (ii), using the effaceability properties of the non-commutative \(H^1\), an argument which on the other hand does not yield a result, as above, for a fixed \(\bar F\).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 6.13

The most important case where the conditions of 6.5 (i) (ii) (iii) are fulfilled is the one considered in 5.5, which will be proved in the following exposé using the reductions made in the present exposé. Another interesting case (where \(h\) is not a closed immersion as in 5.5) will be studied in XV. Let us also point out the case, fairly close to 5.5, where \(X\) is the spectrum of a noetherian ring, separated and complete for the topology defined by an ideal \(J\), and where \(Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A/J)\) is the closed subscheme of \(X\) defined by \(J\). One then verifies directly the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)) in the form b'') (EGA IV 18.3.2); it is very plausible that the conditions of 6.5 (iii) are also verified for every \(n\), i.e. that for every sheaf of torsion \(F\) on \(X\), the homomorphisms \(H^n(X,F) \to H^n(Y,F|Y)\) are bijective. One can make considerably more general conjectures, connected with a generalization to non-local schemes of the henselization construction. First of all, let us note that no example is known, \(h\) being a closed immersion, where the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (iii) are not satisfied (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)) when the "resp." condition of 6.5 (i) is, that is, when the pair \((X,Y)\) is a henselian pair in the terminology of (EGA IV 18.5.5); one may therefore conjecture that such a pair satisfies the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (iii) (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\), every \(n\)). On the other hand, one may ask under what conditions the following property for a pair \((X,Y)\) consisting of a quasi-complete and quasi-separated scheme \(X\) and a closed subscheme \(Y\) implies that the pair is henselian:

(*) For every scheme \(X'\) étale over \(X\), setting \(Y' = X' \times_X Y\), the canonical map \(\Gamma(Y'/Y) \to \Gamma(X'/X)\) is bijective.

(Cf. EGA IV 18.5.4 b)). This condition is evidently a priori weaker than the henselian condition 6.5 (i); it is even strictly weaker, for it is verified for example if \(X\) is a normal irreducible projective scheme of dimension \(\geq 2\) over a field \(k\), and \(Y\) a hyperplane section of \(X\) (as follows easily from SGA 2 XII 2.1, where one takes \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\)), but evidently the pair \((X,Y)\) is not henselian. It is possible on the other hand that if \(X\) is affine, condition (*) implies that \((X,Y)\) is a henselian pair; if this were so, for every affine scheme \(X\) and every closed subset \(Y\) of \(X\), a process of étale localization along \(Y\), analogous to that of the henselization of local rings, should allow one to associate to it a henselian pair \((X',Y)\), where \(X'\) is "pro-étale" over \(X\). Another hypothesis on \((X,Y)\) (suggested by results of Hironaka and Rossi on the contractibility of certain subvarieties of algebraic varieties), which might perhaps allow one to deduce the henselian property from the weaker property (*), is the following: the immersion \(Y \to X\) is regular of codimension 1, and the conormal sheaf \(\underline{N}_{Y/X} = \underline{J}/\underline{J}^2\) (where \(\underline{J}\) is the ideal defining \(Y\) in \(X\)) is an ample invertible sheaf on \(Y\). (NB. In the case of the counterexample considered above, this conormal sheaf was on the contrary anti-ample, i.e. its inverse being ample).
