blocks.html: 7. A variant of Chow's Lemma (*)
We shall need the following variant of (EGA II 5.6.1), freed of all noetherian or irreducibility hypotheses.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.1

Let \(S\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme, and \(f : X \to S\) a separated morphism of finite type, with \(X\) non-empty. There exists a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & \bar X \ar[l]_{\pi} \ar[dl]^{\bar f} \\ S & } \] with \(\pi\) projective and \(\bar f\) quasi-projective, and a non-empty open subset \(U\) of \(X\), such that \(\pi\) induces an isomorphism from \(\bar U = U \times_X \bar X = \pi^{-1}(U)\) onto \(U\).

Proof. Let us first note: Let \(i : X' \to X\) be a closed subscheme of \(X/S\) and \(V \subset X'\) a subscheme open in \(X\) and dense in \(X'\). If the lemma is true for \(X'\), it is true for \(X\). Indeed, let \[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[d]_{f'} & \bar X' \ar[l]_{\pi'} \ar[dl]^{\bar f'} \\ S & } \] be a diagram as in the statement, and \(U' \neq \emptyset\) an open subset of \(X'\) such that \(\pi'\) induces an isomorphism \(\bar U' = \pi'^{-1}(U') \to U'\). Since \(V\) is dense in \(X'\), \(U' \cap V \neq \emptyset\) and one may therefore replace \(U'\) by this open subset. Then \(U'\) is an open subset of \(X\), and one sets \(\pi = i\pi'\), \(\bar f = \bar f'\), \(U = U'\).

Now there exists a finite covering of \(X\) by non-empty affine open subsets \(U_k\), \(k=1,\ldots,n\); from the hypothesis on \(S\) it follows that each \(U_k \to S\) is quasi-affine, and a fortiori quasi-compact. Let us prove the theorem for all \(X\), by induction on \(n\): If the intersection \(U\) of the \(U_k\) is dense in \(X\) one may copy the proof of (EGA II 5.6, B, C, D), taking into account the modifications of the notation. If the intersection is non-empty, one reduces to the case where it is dense by replacing \(X\) by the closure \(X'\) of \(U\) (cf. above), and \(U_k\) by \(U'_k = U_k \cap X'\). Suppose finally that \(U\) is empty and let us choose \(r\), \(1 \leq r \leq n\), such that \(V = \bigcap_{k=1}^{r} U_k \neq \emptyset\) but \(V \cap U_{r+1} = \emptyset\) — this is evidently possible since \(U_1 \neq \emptyset\). We may now replace \(X\) by the closure \(X'\) of \(V\) and the \(U\) by the non-empty \(U_k \cap V\). Since then \(U_{r+1} \cap V\) is empty, one obtains the result by the induction hypothesis.

footnotes.html: (*) The reader interested in the statements of par. 5 only in the noetherian case may omit the reading of the present number.

blocks.html: 8. Final reductions

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.1

To prove one of the statements 5.1 (i) (ii) (iii), it suffices to do so when one assumes \(f\) projective and \(S\) noetherian.

Suppose first 5.1 proved for \(f\) projective; let us show how one concludes from it the same statement for arbitrary \(f\). Using 6.1, we are reduced to the case of 5.5, with \(S\) strictly local. Let us now apply 6.10 taking \(Y = X_o\). Given \((\xi,X')\) as stated in 6.10, we apply Chow's lemma 7.1 to find an \(S\)-morphism \(p : \bar X \to X'\), with \(\bar X\) projective over \(S\), such that \(p(\bar X)\) contains a non-empty open subset of \(X'\) (condition 1°) of 6.10). Since \(p\) is projective, by hypothesis the base change homomorphisms for \((p,h)\) are isomorphisms (condition 2°) of 6.10). Finally, since \(X\) is projective over \(S\), by hypothesis the inclusion morphism \(\bar Y = \bar X_o \to \bar X\) induces an isomorphism for the cohomology groups \(H^i(\bar X, \bar F) \to H^i(\bar X_o, \bar h^*(\bar F))\), (condition 3°) of 6.10). Hence the conditions of 6.10 are indeed satisfied, whence the conclusion.

Let us now show that to verify one of the three statements 5.1 for every situation \((f,F,g)\), with \(f\) projective, one may assume moreover that \(S\) is noetherian. For this, one notes that one may assume, thanks to 6.1, that \(S\) is strictly local and that \(S' \to S\) is the inclusion of the closed point, and one is reduced to verifying the statement 5.5 with \(S\) strictly local. Moreover, since \(X\) embeds in the standard projective scheme \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), one may (thanks to the compatibility 4.4 (ii)) replace \(X\) by \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), \(F\) by its image in \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), which brings us to the case where \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\). Note that \(A\) is the filtered inductive limit of noetherian henselian local subrings \(A_i\) such that the inclusion homomorphism \(A_i \to A\) is local: take the strict henselizations of the finite-type sub-\(\underline{\mathbb{Z}}\)-algebras of \(A\) at the prime ideals induced by the maximal ideal of \(A\). Under these conditions, the residue field \(k\) of \(A\) is also the inductive limit of the fields \(k\) of the \(A_i\) (EGA IV 5.13.1). Let \(S_i = \operatorname{Spec}(A_i)\), \(X_i = \mathbf{P}^r_{S_i}\), and suppose given an inductive system \((F_i)\) of sheaves of sets (resp. ...) on the \(X_i\) as in VII 5.7, and let \(F\) be the sheaf it defines on \(X\). Let \(F_{io}\) (resp. \(F_o\)) be the sheaf induced by \(F_i\) on the fibre \(X_{io}\) of the closed point \(s_i\) of \(S_i\) (resp. on the fibre \(X_o\) of the closed point \(s\) of \(S\)). Then one has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \varinjlim_i H^n(X_i, F_i) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^n(X, F) \ar[d] \\ \varinjlim_i H^n(X_{io}, F_{io}) \ar[r] & H^n(X_o, F_o) , } \] whose two horizontal arrows are isomorphisms, by virtue of VII 5.7. Consequently, to prove that the second vertical arrow is an isomorphism, it suffices to prove it for the first, so it suffices to prove that the homomorphisms \(H^n(X_i, F_i) \to H^n(X_{io}, F_{io})\) are isomorphisms. On the other hand, every sheaf of sets (resp. ...) \(F\) on \(X\) is isomorphic to the limit of an inductive system as above, taking for example \(F_i = u_{i*}(F)\), \(u_i : X \to X_i\) being the canonical morphism, by virtue of ( 5.2) and (IX 1.6 (iii)). This completes the proof of 8.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.2

Theorem 5.1 (i) is true.
Indeed, it suffices to combine 8.1, the criterion 6.5 (i) b''), and 5.8.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.3

To prove one of the statements 5.1 (i) (ii) (iii), it suffices to do so when one assumes \(f\) projective of relative dimension \(\leq 1\), and \(S\) noetherian.

Indeed, we already know by 8.1 that one may restrict to the case \(f\) projective, \(S\) noetherian, and an argument already pointed out allows us to assume moreover that \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\). We then proceed by induction on \(r\), noting that the theorem is true by hypothesis for \(r = 1\). One may therefore assume \(r \geq 2\), and the theorem proved for \(\mathbf{P}^{r-1}_S \to S\) (every base \(S\)). Consider \(Z = \mathbf{P}^{r-2}_S\) as embedded in \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\) in the usual way, and let \(p : \bar X \to X\) be obtained by blowing up \(Z\) in \(X\). An immediate computation (cf. EGA V) shows that one has a natural morphism \(p_1 : \bar X \to X_1 = \mathbf{P}^1_S\), which makes \(\bar X\) an \(X_1\)-scheme locally isomorphic to \(\mathbf{P}^{r-1}_{X_1}\) (it is the projective bundle over \(X_1\) associated with a suitable locally free sheaf of rank \(r\) on \(X_1\)). On the other hand, the fibres of \(p\) are of dimension \(\leq 1\), as are those of \(f_1 : X_1 \to S\). We may therefore apply the hypothesis, and the induction hypothesis, to the three morphisms \(p, p_1, f_1\) in the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \bar X \ar[dl]_{p} \ar[dr]^{p_1} & \\ X \ar[dr]_{f} & & X_1 \ar[dl]^{f_1} \\ & S & } \] Since \(p\) is surjective, the lemma 6.8 reduces us to proving 5.1 for the composite \(\bar f = fp = f_1 p_1\). Now we can already apply 5.1 to the two morphisms \(f_1\) and \(p_1\). Taking 6.11 into account, one concludes that 5.1 is true also for their composite \(f_1 p_1\). This completes the proof of 8.3.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.4

To prove 5.1 (ii), it suffices to prove the "specialization theorem for the fundamental group" 5.9 bis, in the case where \(f\) is projective of relative dimension \(\leq 1\), and where \(S\) is strictly local noetherian.
This indeed follows immediately from 8.3, 6.1 and 6.5 (ii) (criterion b)).
We shall prove the specialization theorem directly, in case 8.4, in the following exposé (XIII 2).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.5

To prove 5.1 (iii), it suffices to prove 5.1 (ii) and, moreover, the following proposition (which will be proved in the following exposé (XIII 3) or (EGA IV 21.9.12)):

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.6

Let \(S\) be henselian and noetherian, \(f : X \to S\) projective of relative dimension \(\leq 1\), and \(X_o\) the closed fibre of \(X/S\). For every scheme \(Z\), let \(\operatorname{Pic} Z = H^1(Z, (\mathbb{G}_m)_Z)\) be the Picard group of \(Z\). The restriction morphism \[ \operatorname{Pic} X \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic} X_o \] is surjective.

Proof of 8.5. By 6.5 (iii) and 8.2, it suffices to prove that \[ \varphi^q : H^q(X, \mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}) \longrightarrow H^q(X_o, \mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}) \] is surjective for every \(q \geq 1\), and every prime number \(\ell\). Now surjectivity is known if \(q = 1\), by 5.1 (ii). Moreover, since \(X_o\) is a projective scheme of dimension \(\leq 1\) over a separably closed field \(k\), we have \[ H^q(X_o, \mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}) = 0 \] if \(q > 2\) in the case \(\ell \neq \operatorname{car} k\) (X 4.3), and if \(q > 1\) in the case \(\ell = \operatorname{car} k\) (X 5.2). Surjectivity is thus trivial for these values of \(q\)!

It remains to treat the case \(q = 2\) and \(\ell \neq \operatorname{car} k\). Set \(n = \ell^\nu\). Since the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity \((\mu_n)_S\) is locally isomorphic to \((\mathbb{Z}/n)_S\), and \(S\) is strictly local, there exists a (non-canonical) isomorphism \((\mu_n)_S \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_S\), whence \((\mu_n)_X \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_X\).

By Kummer theory IX 3.2 applied to \(X\) and \(X_o\), we have a morphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{Pic} X \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\varepsilon} & H^2(X, \mu_n) \ar[r] \ar[d]^{\varphi^2} & H^2(X, \mathbb{G}_m) \ar[d] \\ \operatorname{Pic} X_o \ar[r] & H^2(X_o, \mu_n) \ar[r] & H^2(X_o, \mathbb{G}_m) . } \] Now \(H^2(X_o, \mathbb{G}_m) = 0\) by IX 4.6. Hence the surjectivity of \(\varepsilon\) implies that of \(\varphi^2\), whence the lemma.
